\chapter{Why, and Because}
\label{ch:mr-why-because}
\hlchaptermodality{34}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask why in Marathi, answer it with a whole reason clause after kaaran, and use the comma in a written list and after a named reader.}

Complete MR-R34-reasons and take both turns unaided: ask kaa?, then answer with the claim first and the reason after kaaran.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kā …?]{\mr{का} (kā) — why}

\label{lesson:MR-C34-kaa-why}



\begin{quote}
Retrieve the two items before this one by name: the particle \textbf{\mr{का}} that turns a statement into a yes-or-no question, and the single \textbf{?} that marks it on the page. Say a question with both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{का} at the front}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{का}?} — \emph{kā?} — \textbf{why?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{का} \mr{आवडते}?} — \emph{kā āvaḍte?} — \textbf{Why do you like it?}
\end{quote}

The same two letters you have just learned to hang on the end mean \textbf{why} when they stand at the front, or on their own. That is not a coincidence and it is not an accident of spelling: both come from the Sanskrit question stem \textbf{\mr{क}-} (\emph{ka-}), which also built \textbf{\mr{काय}} (\textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\mr{कसा}} (\textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}). Marathi's whole question system is one syllable with different tails, and the same Indo-European \textbf{k-} is under Latin \emph{quis} and English \emph{who}.

Position is what keeps the two apart, so it is worth saying both aloud back to back:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\mr{मराठी} \mr{आवडते} \mr{का}?} — \emph{do you like Marathi?} (particle, at the end)
  \item \textbf{\mr{मराठी} \mr{का} \mr{आवडते}?} — \emph{why do you like Marathi?} (question word, in front of the verb)
\end{itemize}

Said on its own, \textbf{\mr{का}?} is a complete turn: it is how you ask someone to explain what they have just said.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{marāṭhī āvaḍte kā?} then \emph{marāṭhī kā āvaḍte?}
  \item \emph{kā?} on its own, as a whole turn
  \item the three k-words together — \emph{kāy}, \emph{kasā}, \emph{kā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\mr{का}} mean at the front of a sentence? (\textbf{Why}.) And at the end? (\textbf{It makes a yes-or-no question}.) What decides which? (\textbf{Where it stands}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{का}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kāraṇ]{\mr{कारण} (kāraṇ) — because}

\label{lesson:MR-C34-kaaran}



\begin{quote}
You can now ask \textbf{\mr{का}?}. Ask it out loud. Then notice that you have no way whatever to answer it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \mr{कारण} takes a whole sentence after it}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{मराठी} \mr{शिकतो} \mr{कारण} \mr{मला} \mr{मराठी} \mr{आवडते}.} — \emph{mī marāṭhī shikto kāraṇ malā marāṭhī āvaḍte.} — \textbf{I am learning Marathi because I like Marathi.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{आणि}}, \textbf{\mr{किंवा}} and \textbf{\mr{पण}} put two things side by side as equals. \textbf{\mr{कारण}} does something new: everything after it is \emph{subordinate} — it exists only to explain the half in front. That is the first time in this book that one Marathi clause has been put \textbf{inside} the job of another.

The order is fixed and it is the useful way round: \textbf{the claim first, the reason second}. English can lead with \emph{because}; Marathi's ordinary sentence does not.

\textbf{\mr{कारण}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{कारण}} (\emph{kāraṇa}), \textquotedblleft{}a cause,\textquotedblright{} built on the root \textbf{\mr{कृ}} (\emph{kṛ-}), \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{} — the same \textbf{\mr{कृ}} inside \textbf{\mr{करणे}}, the verb this book gave you for \emph{to do}. Marathi's \emph{because} is, at root, \emph{the doing of it}.

A short answer works too. Asked \textbf{\mr{का}?}, you may reply with \textbf{\mr{कारण}} and one clause, and nothing else is needed.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kā?} then answer it with \emph{kāraṇ …}
  \item \emph{malā chahā āvaḍto paṇ dūdh āvaḍat nāhī} — equals — then \emph{mī marāṭhī shikto kāraṇ malā marāṭhī āvaḍte} — not equals
  \item which verb \textbf{\mr{कारण}} is related to — \emph{karṇe}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which half comes first in a Marathi \textbf{\mr{कारण}} sentence? (\textbf{The claim; the reason follows}.) How is \textbf{\mr{कारण}} unlike \textbf{\mr{पण}}? (\textbf{\mr{पण} joins two equals; \mr{कारण} puts one clause underneath the other}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%B0\%E0\%A4\%A3}{Wiktionary: \mr{कारण}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[svalpaviraam]{, — the mark that carries a list}

\label{lesson:MR-W34-comma}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\mr{चहा} \mr{आणि} \mr{दूध} \mr{आणि} \mr{पाणी}}. Three things, two \textbf{\mr{आणि}}. Out loud it is clumsy; on paper it is worse.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script: the comma does the joining work for all but the last pair}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{चहा}, \mr{दूध} \mr{आणि} \mr{पाणी}}
\end{quote}

Marathi writes the comma exactly as English does: it stands in for the joining word between every pair except the last, where \textbf{\mr{आणि}} is written out. The mark is the same shape you already know from the Latin alphabet, sitting on the baseline below the letters — not hanging from the headline like a Devanagari sign.

It has one more everyday job, and it is the one the writing task needs:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{नमस्कार} \mr{मीरा}, \mr{मी} \mr{अरुण}.} — \emph{namaskār Mīrā, mī Aruṇ.}
\end{quote}

A comma after the person you are addressing. Every message that opens by naming its reader wants one.

Marathi's own name for it, \textbf{\mr{स्वल्पविराम}}, means \textquotedblleft{}small pause,\textquotedblright{} which is a better description than \emph{comma} — the mark tells the eye to hesitate, not to stop.

\subsection*{Writing — copy, then place}
Write \textbf{\mr{चहा}, \mr{दूध} \mr{आणि} \mr{पाणी}} once. Then write \textbf{\mr{नमस्कार} \mr{मीरा},} and check that the comma sits on the baseline, after the name.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In a written list of three, how many \textbf{\mr{आणि}} do you write, and where? (\textbf{One, before the last item}.) What does the comma's Marathi name mean? (\textbf{Small pause}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kā? — kāraṇ …]{Two turns: why, and because}

\label{lesson:MR-R34-reasons}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{का}} at the end asks yes-or-no. \textbf{\mr{का}} at the front asks why. Say one of each before you go on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{marāṭhī āvaḍte kā?} — \emph{ho} — \emph{kā?} — \emph{kāraṇ …}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mī marāṭhī shikto kāraṇ malā marāṭhī āvaḍte}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \emph{chahā, dūdh āṇi pāṇī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which joining word puts one clause underneath another? (\textbf{\mr{कारण}}.) Which half of a \textbf{\mr{कारण}} sentence comes first? (\textbf{The claim}.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
